2.06 · Matrix and notation primer: the linear algebra an inversion actually uses¶

Before this: 2.03 (variance, covariance, the covariance matrix and the Gaussian ellipse). You will be able to: read the shape and units of every symbol in $\mathbf d = \mathbf G\mathbf m + \mathbf e$; say what a transpose, an inverse and a determinant do; read a covariance matrix through its eigenvalues and tell a valid one from a singular or impossible one; use the Cholesky factor to draw correlated noise, whiten residuals, solve systems and compute log-determinants, and recognise when it fails; solve a linear system without forming an inverse; read rank and null space off a singular value decomposition. Optional sections: 5e (how the Cholesky factorisation fails) and 8 (log-determinant overflow) on a first reading.

Every later notebook writes the inverse problem with vectors and matrices. This one collects the few operations that keep coming back, each on a tiny fault with a handful of slip patches and GPS stations, so that every number can be checked by eye. It is a reference: read it once now, and come back when a later notebook uses a word from the list below.

Words this notebook defines: scalar, vector, matrix, Green's function, matrix-vector product, transpose, dot product, gradient, inverse, determinant, singular matrix, eigenvalue and eigenvector, positive definite and semi-definite, Cholesky factor, pivot, triangular solve, whitening, jitter, round-off, condition number, least squares, normal equations, QR factorisation, singular value decomposition (SVD), rank, null space, log-determinant.

In [1]:
import sys, pathlib, time
sys.path.insert(0, str(pathlib.Path.cwd().parent))
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import scipy.linalg as sl
import bayeskit as bk
from bayeskit import plotting as BP, style as S

T0 = time.time()
np.set_printoptions(precision=4, suppress=True)


def patch_disp(x, z1, z2):
    """Surface displacement per unit slip of an antiplane patch between depths z1 and z2 (screw dislocation)."""
    return (np.arctan(z2 / x) - np.arctan(z1 / x)) / np.pi

1. Notation, shapes and units¶

In plain words. A scalar is one number, a vector is a list of numbers, a matrix is a table. The forward model of a linear inverse problem says: the data are a weighted sum of the unknowns. Writing it with a matrix is just bookkeeping for "station $i$ sees $G_{i1}$ times the slip of patch 1 plus $G_{i2}$ times the slip of patch 2". Each column of $\mathbf G$ is the fingerprint one patch leaves on all stations; each row is what one station sees of all patches. The entries are Green's functions: the displacement at one station caused by unit slip on one patch, computed once from a physical model of the Earth.

The example fault here is the simplest one used in this course: a long vertical strike-slip fault in a uniform elastic half-space, with slip only along strike, so that the ground moves only parallel to the fault ("antiplane" motion). Its Green's functions have a closed form, the screw dislocation (Segall 2010): a patch between depths $z_1$ and $z_2$ moves a surface point at distance $x$ by $[\arctan(z_2/x) - \arctan(z_1/x)]/\pi$ per unit slip.

Precisely. The notation used in every notebook:

symbol what it is shape units in this notebook
$a$, $\sigma$, $\lambda$ (italic) scalars 1 various
$\mathbf d$ (bold lower case) data vector $N_d$ mm
$\mathbf m$ model (unknowns) vector $N_m$ m of slip
$\mathbf G$ (bold upper case) forward operator: Green's functions $N_d\times N_m$ mm per m of slip
$\mathbf e$ noise vector $N_d$ mm
$\mathbf C_d$ data (noise) covariance $N_d\times N_d$ mm²
$\mathbf C_m$ prior covariance of the model $N_m\times N_m$ m²
$\mathbf C_p$ prediction (model-error) covariance (2.13) $N_d\times N_d$ mm²
$\mathbf C_\chi = \mathbf C_d + \mathbf C_p$ total misfit covariance (2.13) $N_d\times N_d$ mm²
$\mathbf r = \mathbf d - \mathbf G\mathbf m$ residual: what the model fails to explain $N_d$ mm
$\mathbf I$ identity matrix: ones on the diagonal, zeros elsewhere

The matrix-vector product $\mathbf G\mathbf m$ has entries $(\mathbf G\mathbf m)_i = \sum_j G_{ij}m_j$. It is defined only when the number of columns of $\mathbf G$ equals the length of $\mathbf m$, and the result has the length of the data. Checking shapes and units is the cheapest bug test there is: $(N_d\times N_m)(N_m)\to(N_d)$, and (mm per m)(m) = mm.

Worked example. Three stations at 3, 10 and 30 km from the fault; two patches, 0-10 km and 10-20 km deep; slip 2 m on the shallow patch and 1 m on the deep one.

In [2]:
x_st = np.array([3.0, 10.0, 30.0])                    # km from the fault
z2 = np.array([0.0, 10.0, 20.0])                      # patch edges (km)
G = 1000.0 * np.array([[patch_disp(x, z2[j], z2[j + 1]) for j in range(2)] for x in x_st])   # mm per m
m_ex = np.array([2.0, 1.0])                           # m
d_ex = G @ m_ex
print("G (rows: stations at 3, 10, 30 km; columns: shallow, deep patch), mm per m of slip:\n", G)
print(f"shapes: G {G.shape}, m {m_ex.shape}, d = G m {d_ex.shape}")
print("d = G m (mm):", d_ex)
print("the same, column by column: 2 x column 1 + 1 x column 2 =", 2 * G[:, 0] + 1 * G[:, 1])
print("the same, row by row (station 1): G[0,0]*2 + G[0,1]*1 =", G[0, 0] * 2 + G[0, 1] * 1)

saved figures/2-06_forward_product.png

How to read it. (a) The geometry. (b) The matrix: each entry is the displacement at one station per metre of slip on one patch. The shallow patch (column 1) is seen strongly by the near station and weakly far away; the deep patch (column 2) is seen more evenly. (c) The prediction is the sum of the two columns, each scaled by its slip.

Common misreadings.

  • "Matrix multiplication is something abstract." Here it is a weighted sum of fingerprints; that is all $\mathbf G\mathbf m$ ever is, for 2 patches or for 2,000.
  • "Units do not matter as long as the code runs." Mixing m and mm in $\mathbf G$ changes the answer by a factor of 1000 without any error message; the unit check above catches it.

2. The transpose: sending data back to the parameters¶

In plain words. $\mathbf G$ takes slip to data. Its transpose $\mathbf G^\top$ (the same table with rows and columns swapped, $(\mathbf G^\top)_{ij} = G_{ji}$) goes the other way: it takes something defined at the stations, such as a residual, and tells each patch how much of it that patch could explain. That is why $\mathbf G^\top$ appears in every gradient and every normal equation.

Precisely. The dot product of two vectors of the same length is $\langle\mathbf a,\mathbf b\rangle = \mathbf a^\top\mathbf b = \sum_i a_ib_i$: large when they point the same way, zero when they are perpendicular. For any slip vector $\mathbf m$ and any data-space vector $\mathbf y$, $\langle\mathbf G\mathbf m,\mathbf y\rangle = \langle\mathbf m,\mathbf G^\top\mathbf y\rangle$ (the "dot-product test", used to check codes that implement $\mathbf G^\top$ separately; 2.22). The gradient of a function of several unknowns is the vector of its partial derivatives: it points in the direction in which the function rises fastest. The misfit $\chi^2(\mathbf m) = \mathbf r^\top\mathbf C_d^{-1}\mathbf r$ with $\mathbf r = \mathbf d - \mathbf G\mathbf m$ ($\mathbf C_d^{-1}$ is the inverse of the noise covariance, section 3) has gradient $-2\,\mathbf G^\top\mathbf C_d^{-1}\mathbf r$: the noise-weighted residual sent back through $\mathbf G^\top$.

Worked example. Data made from the slip of section 1 plus noise (σ = 2 mm), compared with a guess of 1 m on each patch; the gradient is checked against finite differences (the change in χ² for a tiny change of one slip value).

In [4]:
sig = 2.0                                                             # mm
d_obs = d_ex + sig * np.random.default_rng(3).standard_normal(3)
m_guess = np.array([1.0, 1.0])
r = d_obs - G @ m_guess
Cd = sig ** 2 * np.eye(3)
grad = -2 * G.T @ np.linalg.solve(Cd, r)
chi2 = lambda m: (d_obs - G @ m) @ np.linalg.solve(Cd, d_obs - G @ m)
h = 1e-6
grad_fd = np.array([(chi2(m_guess + h * e) - chi2(m_guess - h * e)) / (2 * h) for e in np.eye(2)])
print("observed d (mm):", d_obs, "  residual r = d - G m_guess (mm):", r)
print("gradient of chi^2 from G^T:", grad, "  from finite differences:", grad_fd)
y_rand = np.random.default_rng(4).standard_normal(3)
m_rand = np.random.default_rng(5).standard_normal(2)
print(f"dot-product test: <G m, y> = {(G @ m_rand) @ y_rand:.12f},  <m, G^T y> = {m_rand @ (G.T @ y_rand):.12f}")

observed d (mm): [863.9151 597.3051 290.4196]   residual r = d - G m_guess (mm): [411.3083 244.8887 103.2526]
gradient of chi^2 from G^T: [-119646.2567  -26248.3422]   from finite differences: [-119646.2567  -26248.3422]
dot-product test: <G m, y> = -12.627709236000,  <m, G^T y> = -12.627709236000

saved figures/2-06_transpose.png

How to read it. (a) The guess under-predicts every station (positive residuals). (b) The same residuals sent back through $\mathbf G^\top$: both patches should slip more, the shallow one more strongly, because the near station, which sees mainly the shallow patch, has the largest residual. The printed gradient equals the finite-difference one.

Common misreadings.

  • "$\mathbf G^\top$ is the inverse of $\mathbf G$." It is not; it does not undo $\mathbf G$ (it does not even have the right units). It only says which direction in parameter space reduces the misfit.

3. The inverse and the determinant¶

In plain words. A square matrix $\mathbf A$ moves points around: it stretches, squeezes, tilts and possibly flips space. Its inverse $\mathbf A^{-1}$ moves them back, so that $\mathbf A^{-1}\mathbf A = \mathbf I$. The determinant $\det\mathbf A$ (also written $\lvert\mathbf A\rvert$) is the factor by which $\mathbf A$ changes areas (in 2-D) or volumes (in more dimensions), with a minus sign if it flips orientation. If some direction is squashed flat, the area becomes zero, $\det\mathbf A = 0$, and nothing can undo the squashing: the matrix is singular and has no inverse.

Precisely. For $\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix}a & b\\ c & d\end{pmatrix}$: $\det\mathbf A = ad - bc$ and $\mathbf A^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad-bc}\begin{pmatrix}d & -b\\ -c & a\end{pmatrix}$. In general $\det(\mathbf A\mathbf B) = \det\mathbf A\,\det\mathbf B$, and the determinant is the product of the eigenvalues (section 4). Why it matters here: the inverse of the noise covariance weights the misfit (section 2), and the determinant of a covariance sets the normalising constant of the Gaussian density (2.03), which matters whenever a noise level is estimated (2.30). In computer code, inverses are almost never formed explicitly (section 6).

Worked example. The unit square mapped by an invertible matrix and by a singular one.

In [6]:
A_ok = np.array([[1.5, 0.6], [0.3, 1.0]])
A_sing = np.array([[1.5, 0.75], [0.6, 0.3]])                         # second column = half the first
for nm, A_ in [("invertible", A_ok), ("singular", A_sing)]:
    print(f"{nm:10s} A = {A_.tolist()}: det = {np.linalg.det(A_):.4f}", end="")
    if abs(np.linalg.det(A_)) > 1e-12:
        print(f";  A^-1 = {np.round(np.linalg.inv(A_), 4).tolist()};  A^-1 A = {np.round(np.linalg.inv(A_) @ A_, 12).tolist()}")
    else:
        print("  -> no inverse: the whole plane is squashed onto one line")

invertible A = [[1.5, 0.6], [0.3, 1.0]]: det = 1.3200;  A^-1 = [[0.7576, -0.4545], [-0.2273, 1.1364]];  A^-1 A = [[1.0, -0.0], [0.0, 1.0]]
singular   A = [[1.5, 0.75], [0.6, 0.3]]: det = 0.0000  -> no inverse: the whole plane is squashed onto one line
In [7]:
sq = np.array([[0, 1, 1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 1, 1, 0.0]])
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
for ax, A_, ttl in [(axs[0], A_ok, "(a) Invertible: area scaled by det A"), (axs[1], A_sing, "(b) Singular: det A = 0")]:
    ax.fill(sq[0], sq[1], color=S.MUTED, alpha=0.25, label="unit square (area 1)")
    im_ = A_ @ sq
    ax.fill(im_[0], im_[1], color=S.BLUE, alpha=0.35, label=f"A × square (area {abs(np.linalg.det(A_)):.2f})")
    ax.plot(im_[0], im_[1], color=S.BLUE, lw=1.4)
    for k, c in enumerate([S.ORANGE, S.AQUA]):
        ax.annotate("", xy=A_[:, k], xytext=(0, 0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=c, lw=1.6))
    ax.plot([], [], color=S.ORANGE, lw=1.6, label="A × (1, 0) = column 1")
    ax.plot([], [], color=S.AQUA, lw=1.6, label="A × (0, 1) = column 2")
    ax.set_xlim(-0.3, 2.4); ax.set_ylim(-0.3, 1.8); ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_title(ttl); ax.legend(fontsize=7.6, loc="upper left")
fig.tight_layout()
bk.savefig(fig, "2-06_inverse_determinant")
plt.show()

saved figures/2-06_inverse_determinant.png

How to read it. (a) The square becomes a parallelogram spanned by the two columns of $\mathbf A$; its area is $\lvert\det\mathbf A\rvert$ (printed), and $\mathbf A^{-1}$ maps it back. (b) The second column is a multiple of the first, so the parallelogram collapses onto a line: zero area, and many points land on the same image point, so no inverse can tell them apart. That is exactly the situation of slip patterns the stations cannot see (section 7).

Common misreadings.

  • "A tiny determinant means the matrix is nearly singular." Not by itself: scaling all entries by 0.001 makes the determinant tiny without making the matrix any harder to invert. Nearness to singularity is measured by the condition number (section 6).

4. Covariance matrices: eigenvalues, positive-definiteness, and when it fails¶

Reminder (2.03). The variance of a quantity is the average squared distance from its mean; the covariance of two quantities ("co-": varying together) is positive when they rise together and negative when one rises as the other falls. The covariance matrix $\mathbf C$ holds the variances on its diagonal and the covariances off it; it is symmetric, $\mathbf C = \mathbf C^\top$.

In plain words. Every covariance matrix has special directions, its eigenvectors, along which the uncertainty is simply "more" or "less", without any tilt; the amounts are the eigenvalues, the variances along those directions. In two dimensions they are the axes of the uncertainty ellipse. A valid covariance must give every possible combination of the quantities a variance of zero or more, which means every eigenvalue is zero or more.

Precisely. A vector $\mathbf q\ne\mathbf 0$ with $\mathbf C\mathbf q = \lambda\mathbf q$ is an eigenvector and $\lambda$ its eigenvalue. A symmetric $\mathbf C$ has $n$ perpendicular unit eigenvectors, so $\mathbf C = \mathbf Q\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf Q^\top$ (eigen-decomposition) with the eigenvectors as columns of $\mathbf Q$ and the eigenvalues on the diagonal of $\boldsymbol\Lambda$. The variance of any weighted combination $y = \mathbf a^\top\mathbf x$ is $\mathrm{Var}(y) = \mathbf a^\top\mathbf C\mathbf a$ (expand the square of $\sum_i a_i(x_i - \mu_i)$ and average). Since a variance cannot be negative, $\mathbf a^\top\mathbf C\mathbf a\ge 0$ for every $\mathbf a$: $\mathbf C$ is positive semi-definite; all $\lambda\ge 0$. It is positive definite (all $\lambda > 0$; then $\det\mathbf C > 0$, $\mathbf C^{-1}$ exists and so does the Cholesky factor of section 5) when no combination is exactly fixed. Why it matters: the posterior covariance, the noise covariance and the prior covariance all have to be valid in this sense, and inverting, factorising or sampling them fails when they are not.

Worked example (a). The posterior covariance of the two-patch problem with σ = 2 mm and a prior standard deviation of 3 m on each patch, $\mathbf C_{\rm post} = (\mathbf G^\top\mathbf C_d^{-1}\mathbf G + \mathbf C_m^{-1})^{-1}$ (derived in 2.08).

In [8]:
Cm = 9.0 * np.eye(2)                                                     # (3 m)^2
P_post = G.T @ np.linalg.solve(Cd, G) + np.linalg.inv(Cm)                # posterior precision (1/m^2)
C_post = np.linalg.inv(P_post)                                           # 2 x 2 only: fine to invert (section 6)
m_post = C_post @ (G.T @ np.linalg.solve(Cd, d_obs))
lam, Q = np.linalg.eigh(C_post)
fmt = dict(formatter={"float_kind": lambda v: f"{v: .3e}"})
print("posterior mean (m):", m_post, "  true:", m_ex)
print("posterior covariance (m^2):\n", np.array2string(C_post, **fmt))
print("symmetric:", np.allclose(C_post, C_post.T), "  eigenvalues (m^2):", np.array2string(lam, **fmt), "  all > 0:", bool(np.all(lam > 0)))
print("sd of each patch (m):", np.sqrt(np.diag(C_post)),
      "  correlation:", C_post[0, 1] / np.sqrt(C_post[0, 0] * C_post[1, 1]))
print("ellipse half-axes, 1 sd (m):", np.sqrt(lam), " along eigenvectors (columns):\n", Q)
print("check C q = lambda q for the first eigenvector:", np.allclose(C_post @ Q[:, 0], lam[0] * Q[:, 0]))
print(f"check det C = product of eigenvalues: {np.linalg.det(C_post):.4e} vs {np.prod(lam):.4e}")
bad = np.array([[1.0, 1.2], [1.2, 1.0]])
print("a 'covariance' with correlation 1.2:", bad.tolist(), " eigenvalues", np.linalg.eigvalsh(bad), "-> not a covariance")

draws = m_post + rng_e.standard_normal((400, 2)) @ np.linalg.cholesky(C_post).T

    ax.annotate("", xy=m_post + v, xytext=m_post, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=S.ORANGE, lw=1.6))

ax.axhline(0, color=S.AXIS, lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("direction of the combination (degrees)"); ax.set_ylabel("variance of that combination, uᵀCu")
ax.set_title("(b) Positive-definite: every direction has variance > 0")
ax.set_ylim(top=1.35 * max(q_good.max(), q_bad.max()))               # headroom so the legend clears the curves
ax.legend(fontsize=7.8, loc="upper right")
fig.tight_layout()

saved figures/2-06_covariance_ellipse.png

How to read it. (a) The draws fill a tilted ellipse: the two slips trade off (negative correlation, printed), because more shallow slip and less deep slip predict similar data. The orange arrows are the eigenvectors scaled by the square roots of the eigenvalues: the long axis is the poorly constrained combination, the short axis the well constrained one. (b) For every unit direction $\mathbf u$, the variance of the combination $\mathbf u^\top\mathbf m$ is $\mathbf u^\top\mathbf C\mathbf u$. A valid covariance gives a positive value in every direction; the matrix with "correlation" 1.2 goes negative in some directions, so it describes no possible random vector.

Worked example (b): when a covariance is only semi-definite, or not one at all. Each case below is computed:

  1. Perfectly correlated quantities: $x_2 = 2x_1$ exactly. The combination $2x_1 - x_2$ never varies.
  2. A constraint: three proportions that must add up to one (Dirichlet shares, 2.11). Their sum never varies.
  3. Too few samples: a covariance estimated from 5 draws (ensemble members, 2.24) of 10 quantities. Five draws span at most four directions around their mean; the others get zero estimated variance.
  4. A smoothing operator with a null space: the second-difference roughness penalty used in 2.09 does not penalise a constant or a straight-line slip profile at all, so its precision matrix (inverse covariance, 2.08) has two zero eigenvalues: those patterns are completely free.
  5. Hand-built and impossible: correlations +0.9 (A with B), +0.9 (A with C) and −0.9 (B with C).
  6. Round-off: a smooth-field covariance on 30 closely spaced points (squared exponential, 2.12). In exact arithmetic it is positive definite; in floating-point arithmetic its smallest eigenvalues are tiny numbers of either sign.
In [10]:
def eig_report(name, M):
    ev = np.linalg.eigvalsh(M)
    try:
        np.linalg.cholesky(M)
        chol = "succeeds"
    except np.linalg.LinAlgError:
        chol = "FAILS"
    print(f"{name:44s} smallest eigenvalues {np.array2string(np.sort(ev)[:3], precision=3):34s} Cholesky {chol}")
    return ev, chol


cases = {}
cases["1 perfectly correlated (x2 = 2 x1)"] = np.array([[1.0, 2.0], [2.0, 4.0]])
al = np.ones(3)
cases["2 proportions summing to 1 (Dirichlet)"] = (np.diag(al) * al.sum() - np.outer(al, al)) / (al.sum() ** 2 * (al.sum() + 1))
cases["3 from 5 samples of 10 quantities"] = np.cov(np.random.default_rng(0).standard_normal((5, 10)).T)
D2 = np.diff(np.eye(10), 2, axis=0)
cases["4 second-difference precision D^T D"] = D2.T @ D2
cases["5 hand-built correlations (+0.9, +0.9, -0.9)"] = np.array([[1.0, 0.9, 0.9], [0.9, 1.0, -0.9], [0.9, -0.9, 1.0]])
z30 = np.linspace(0.0, 10.0, 30)
K30 = np.exp(-0.5 * ((z30[:, None] - z30[None, :]) / 2.0) ** 2)
cases["6 smooth field, 30 points (round-off)"] = K30
rep = {k: eig_report(k, M) for k, M in cases.items()}

How to read it. Each panel shows the size of every eigenvalue on a log scale; grey bars are zero up to round-off, red ones clearly negative. Cases 1 to 4 are positive semi-definite: valid covariances (or precisions) with exactly zero variance in some direction, because something is fixed or free. Case 5 has a clearly negative eigenvalue: not a covariance at all. Case 6 should be positive definite but has eigenvalues at round-off level, of both signs. Exact zeros are drawn as short stubs. The badges show what that means in practice: the Cholesky factorisation (section 5) fails for some singular cases and, by luck of rounding, succeeds for others (case 2), so success alone does not prove a matrix is safely positive definite. Section 5e shows how the failure happens and the usual fix.

Common misreadings.

  • "The standard deviations on the diagonal are the uncertainty." They are the uncertainty of each quantity alone. The combination along the long axis of (a) is far less certain than either diagonal entry suggests, and the one along the short axis far more certain (eigenvalues printed).
  • "Any symmetric matrix of the right size is a covariance." It must also be positive semi-definite (case 5).
  • "A singular covariance is an error." Often it is a true statement: a constraint (case 2) or a free pattern (case 4). It only becomes a problem when the code needs an inverse or a Cholesky factor.

5. The Cholesky factorisation: a square root of a covariance¶

5a. What it is¶

In plain words. A positive number has a square root. A positive-definite covariance matrix has a "square root" too, the Cholesky factor $\mathbf L$: a lower-triangular matrix (zeros above the diagonal) with $\mathbf C = \mathbf L\mathbf L^\top$. It is built one quantity at a time. The first diagonal entry is the standard deviation of the first quantity. Each later diagonal entry is the standard deviation that is left for that quantity once the parts it shares with the earlier quantities are taken out. That left-over variance, computed at each step, is called the pivot; the factorisation takes its square root, so every pivot must be positive.

Precisely. For $j = 1,\dots,n$: the pivot is $p_j = C_{jj} - \sum_{k<j}L_{jk}^2$, then $L_{jj} = \sqrt{p_j}$ and $L_{ij} = (C_{ij} - \sum_{k<j}L_{ik}L_{jk})/L_{jj}$ for $i > j$. The pivot $p_j$ equals the variance of quantity $j$ conditional on quantities $1,\dots,j-1$ (conditioning, 2.04). It is positive for every $j$ exactly when $\mathbf C$ is positive definite. Why it matters: one factorisation, computed once, gives correlated random draws (5b), whitening (5c), linear solves and the log-determinant (5d); and its failure is the standard alarm for an invalid covariance (5e).

Worked example. Noise at four GPS stations at 3, 10, 18 and 30 km along a profile, with standard deviation 2 mm and a correlation that decays with distance, $C_{ij} = (2\ \text{mm})^2 e^{-\lvert x_i - x_j\rvert/20\ \text{km}}$ (an exponential covariance; 2.14 builds such models from real noise).

In [12]:
def chol_with_pivots(C):
    """Plain Cholesky, column by column, returning L, the pivots, and whether it finished."""
    n = len(C)
    L = np.zeros_like(C, dtype=float)
    piv = []
    for j in range(n):
        p = C[j, j] - L[j, :j] @ L[j, :j]
        piv.append(p)
        if not p > 0:                                         # the square root of the pivot is impossible: stop
            return L, np.array(piv), False
        L[j, j] = np.sqrt(p)
        for i in range(j + 1, n):
            L[i, j] = (C[i, j] - L[i, :j] @ L[j, :j]) / L[j, j]
    return L, np.array(piv), True


x4 = np.array([3.0, 10.0, 18.0, 30.0])
expcov = lambda x, lam_, s: s ** 2 * np.exp(-np.abs(x[:, None] - x[None, :]) / lam_)
C4 = expcov(x4, 20.0, 2.0)
L4, piv4, ok4 = chol_with_pivots(C4)
print("C (mm^2):\n", C4)
print("L (mm), lower triangular:\n", L4)
print("pivots (left-over variances, mm^2):", piv4, "  all > 0:", ok4)
print("check L L^T = C:", np.allclose(L4 @ L4.T, C4), "  same as numpy's cholesky:", np.allclose(L4, np.linalg.cholesky(C4)))
print("L_11 = sd of station 1 =", L4[0, 0], "mm;  station 2: total sd 2 mm, left-over sd after station 1 =", L4[1, 1], "mm")

5b. Use 1: making correlated noise¶

In plain words. A computer easily makes independent standard-normal numbers $\mathbf z$ (mean 0, variance 1, no correlation). Multiplying by $\mathbf L$ mixes them so that the result has exactly the covariance $\mathbf C$: $\mathbf x = \boldsymbol\mu + \mathbf L\mathbf z$. This is how every prior draw, noise realisation and posterior draw of a Gaussian in this course is made.

Precisely. $\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf L\mathbf z) = \mathbf L\,\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf z)\,\mathbf L^\top = \mathbf L\mathbf I\mathbf L^\top = \mathbf C$. In two dimensions, $x_1 = L_{11}z_1$ and $x_2 = L_{21}z_1 + L_{22}z_2$: the second quantity borrows part of the first one's randomness (that is the correlation) and adds its own.

Worked example. Stations 1 and 2 of 5a (3 and 10 km).

In [14]:

5c. Use 2: whitening¶

In plain words. Correlated noise is hard to think about; independent noise of unit size is easy. Whitening runs 5b backwards: $\mathbf L^{-1}\mathbf r$ turns correlated residuals into independent ones with standard deviation 1 (the name comes from "white noise", noise without correlation). The misfit is then just a sum of squares.

Precisely. If $\mathbf e\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\mathbf C)$ then $\mathbf L^{-1}\mathbf e\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I)$, and $\chi^2 = \mathbf r^\top\mathbf C^{-1}\mathbf r = \lVert\mathbf L^{-1}\mathbf r\rVert^2$. The product $\mathbf L^{-1}\mathbf r$ is computed by a triangular solve of $\mathbf L\mathbf y = \mathbf r$: because $\mathbf L$ is triangular, its first equation has one unknown, the second two (one already known), and so on ("forward substitution"); no inverse is formed.

Worked example. GPS noise at three stations with an independent part (2 mm per station) and a common-mode part shared by all three (3 mm), as happens when a reference-frame error moves the whole network.

In [16]:
s_w, s_c = 2.0, 3.0
Cd_c = s_w ** 2 * np.eye(3) + s_c ** 2 * np.ones((3, 3))
L = np.linalg.cholesky(Cd_c)
E = np.random.default_rng(11).standard_normal((5000, 3)) @ L.T          # 5000 noise vectors with covariance Cd_c
W = sl.solve_triangular(L, E.T, lower=True).T                             # whitened
print("C_d with common mode (mm^2):\n", Cd_c)
print("Cholesky factor L (mm):\n", L)
print("sample covariance of the raw noise:\n", np.cov(E.T))
print("sample covariance after whitening (should be close to I):\n", np.cov(W.T))
rr = np.array([4.0, 5.0, 3.0])
print(f"chi^2 of a residual {rr.tolist()} mm: with the inverse {rr @ np.linalg.inv(Cd_c) @ rr:.6f}, "
      f"with a triangular solve {np.sum(sl.solve_triangular(L, rr, lower=True) ** 2):.6f}, "
      f"pretending the noise is independent (sigma 2 mm) {np.sum((rr / s_w) ** 2):.6f}")

How to read it. (a) The noise at stations 1 and 2 is strongly correlated: the common mode moves both together. (b) After the triangular solve the cloud is round with unit spread (sample covariances printed). The printed χ² values show what is at stake: the same residual is scored very differently when the common mode is ignored, because a residual that is similar at all stations is cheap under the true covariance (it looks like the common mode) but expensive under independent noise.

Common misreadings.

  • "Whitening changes the data." It changes the coordinates in which residuals are measured, not the information: the χ² is identical with the inverse and with the triangular solve (printed).
  • "A covariance is just a list of standard deviations." Here every station has the same diagonal entry, yet ignoring the off-diagonal common mode changes the misfit of the printed residual by a large factor.

5d. Use 3: solving systems and the log-determinant¶

In plain words. Solving $\mathbf C\mathbf x = \mathbf b$ (needed for every $\mathbf C^{-1}\mathbf b$ in a formula) takes two cheap triangular solves once $\mathbf L$ is known. The determinant comes for free as well: it is the product of the squared diagonal entries of $\mathbf L$, and its logarithm is a sum, which never overflows.

Precisely. $\mathbf C\mathbf x = \mathbf b \iff \mathbf L(\mathbf L^\top\mathbf x) = \mathbf b$: solve $\mathbf L\mathbf y = \mathbf b$ by forward substitution, then $\mathbf L^\top\mathbf x = \mathbf y$ by back substitution (the same idea from the last row upwards). Since $\det\mathbf L = \prod_i L_{ii}$ (triangular) and $\det\mathbf C = (\det\mathbf L)^2$: $\ln\det\mathbf C = 2\sum_i\ln L_{ii}$, the term needed in the Gaussian log-likelihood (section 8).

In [18]:
b4 = np.array([1.0, -2.0, 0.5, 3.0])
y4 = sl.solve_triangular(L4, b4, lower=True)                 # forward substitution
x4s = sl.solve_triangular(L4.T, y4, lower=False)             # back substitution
print("solve C x = b with two triangular solves:", x4s)
print("np.linalg.solve(C, b):                    ", np.linalg.solve(C4, b4))
print(f"ln det C: 2 sum ln L_ii = {2 * np.sum(np.log(np.diag(L4))):.10f},  slogdet = {np.linalg.slogdet(C4)[1]:.10f},  "
      f"ln(det C) = {np.log(np.linalg.det(C4)):.10f}")

5e. How it fails, and the jitter fix¶

In plain words. The factorisation stops the moment a pivot (a left-over variance) is zero or negative, because it cannot take the square root. A zero pivot means some quantity is completely determined by the earlier ones (the matrix is singular). A negative pivot means the matrix claims a negative variance: it is not a covariance. A third failure is purely numerical. Computers store numbers with about 16 significant digits, and every operation rounds the result (round-off). When a pivot should be tiny but positive, round-off can push it below zero. The usual fix is jitter: add a tiny number $\varepsilon$ to the diagonal before factorising.

Precisely. Adding $\varepsilon\mathbf I$ is the same as adding independent noise of variance $\varepsilon$ to every quantity. It raises every eigenvalue by $\varepsilon$ and every pivot by at least $\varepsilon$, so the factorisation succeeds. It is harmless when $\varepsilon$ is far below every variance that matters to the problem (its effect on a covariance is exactly $\varepsilon$ per variance), and it hides a real error when it is used to "fix" a matrix that is invalid (a clearly negative eigenvalue) rather than one that is merely nearly singular.

Worked example. Pivots for four matrices: the station covariance of 5a; the same with a fifth station 1 m away from the second one (two almost identical stations, so almost nothing is left over for the duplicate); the impossible hand-built correlation matrix of section 4; and the 30-point smooth-field covariance of section 4, without and with jitter.

In [19]:

How to read it. (a) For the ordinary station covariance every pivot is a healthy left-over variance. Adding a station 1 m from another leaves almost nothing for the duplicate (a pivot near zero, printed): still positive, but the matrix is nearly singular (huge condition number). For the impossible matrix the third pivot is negative and the factorisation stops. (b) The smooth-field covariance should be positive definite, but its pivots shrink quickly (neighbouring points are almost perfectly correlated) until round-off makes one negative and the factorisation stops. With a jitter of $10^{-10}$ every pivot stays above $\varepsilon$ (dotted line) and the factorisation finishes; the covariance it factorises differs from the original by exactly $\varepsilon$ on the diagonal (printed). The factor itself can differ a lot between two jitter sizes, because in nearly singular directions very different factors give almost the same covariance: compare covariances or distributions, never individual draws.

Common misreadings.

  • "Jitter is a hack that changes the model." It does change the model, by adding a tiny independent noise term. Choose it far below every variance that matters, and say so.
  • "If Cholesky fails, add jitter." First look at the eigenvalues: a clearly negative one (case 5 of section 4) means the matrix is wrong, and jitter would only hide that.

6. Solve, do not invert¶

In plain words. The least-squares answer to $\mathbf d = \mathbf G\mathbf m + \mathbf e$ is the $\mathbf m$ that makes the sum of squared residuals smallest (2.07 derives it and explains why). On paper it is $(\mathbf G^\top\mathbf G)^{-1}\mathbf G^\top\mathbf d$, the solution of the normal equations $\mathbf G^\top\mathbf G\,\mathbf m = \mathbf G^\top\mathbf d$. In a computer, forming that inverse, or even forming $\mathbf G^\top\mathbf G$, throws away accuracy when the problem is close to singular, which inverse problems usually are. The cure costs nothing: ask the library to solve the system, and solve the least-squares problem from $\mathbf G$ itself.

Precisely. The condition number $\kappa(\mathbf G) = s_{\max}/s_{\min}$, the ratio of the largest to the smallest singular value (section 7; for a covariance, the ratio of its largest to smallest eigenvalue), measures how close a matrix is to singular, and bounds how much relative round-off error (about $\epsilon\approx 2\times10^{-16}$ in double precision) can grow in the answer. Forming $\mathbf G^\top\mathbf G$ squares it: $\kappa(\mathbf G^\top\mathbf G) = \kappa(\mathbf G)^2$. The QR factorisation writes $\mathbf G = \mathbf Q\mathbf R$ with orthonormal columns in $\mathbf Q$ (they do not stretch anything) and an upper-triangular $\mathbf R$, so the least-squares problem becomes the triangular system $\mathbf R\mathbf m = \mathbf Q^\top\mathbf d$. Methods that work on $\mathbf G$ directly (QR or SVD: np.linalg.lstsq, scipy.linalg.lstsq) keep the error near $\kappa\,\epsilon$; the normal equations give about $\kappa^2\epsilon$, whether solved by an explicit inverse or by Cholesky. Separately, an explicit inverse leaves a larger residual $\lVert\mathbf A\mathbf x - \mathbf b\rVert$ than a solve of the same system.

Worked example. Test matrices of 40 data and 6 unknowns, built with chosen singular values so that $\kappa(\mathbf G)$ runs from 10 to $10^8$; noise-free data from a known $\mathbf m$, so the error of each method is exact.

In [21]:
rng5 = np.random.default_rng(0)
Nd5, Nm5 = 40, 6
Q1, _ = np.linalg.qr(rng5.standard_normal((Nd5, Nm5)))
Q2, _ = np.linalg.qr(rng5.standard_normal((Nm5, Nm5)))
m5 = rng5.standard_normal(Nm5)
kappas = 10.0 ** np.arange(1, 9)
rel = lambda x: np.linalg.norm(x - m5) / np.linalg.norm(m5)
res = {k: [] for k in ["normal eq., explicit inverse", "normal eq., Cholesky solve", "least squares on G (QR)", "least squares on G (SVD, lstsq)"]}
bres = {"explicit inverse": [], "solve": []}
print(" kappa(G)  inverse(GtG)  Cholesky(GtG)   QR on G    lstsq on G  | residual of GtG x = Gtd: inverse   solve")
for kap in kappas:
    sv5 = np.logspace(0, -np.log10(kap), Nm5)
    G5 = Q1 @ np.diag(sv5) @ Q2.T
    d5 = G5 @ m5
    A5, b5 = G5.T @ G5, G5.T @ d5
    x_inv = np.linalg.inv(A5) @ b5
    try:
        x_cho = sl.cho_solve(sl.cho_factor(A5), b5)
    except np.linalg.LinAlgError:
        x_cho = np.full(Nm5, np.nan)
    q5, r5 = np.linalg.qr(G5)
    x_qr = sl.solve_triangular(r5, q5.T @ d5)
    x_ls = np.linalg.lstsq(G5, d5, rcond=None)[0]
    for k_, x_ in zip(res, [x_inv, x_cho, x_qr, x_ls]):
        res[k_].append(rel(x_))
    nb = lambda x: np.linalg.norm(A5 @ x - b5) / (np.linalg.norm(A5, 2) * np.linalg.norm(x))
    bres["explicit inverse"].append(nb(x_inv)); bres["solve"].append(nb(np.linalg.solve(A5, b5)))
    print(f"  {kap:7.0e}  {res['normal eq., explicit inverse'][-1]:11.1e}  {res['normal eq., Cholesky solve'][-1]:12.1e}  "
          f"{res['least squares on G (QR)'][-1]:9.1e}  {res['least squares on G (SVD, lstsq)'][-1]:10.1e}  | "
          f"{bres['explicit inverse'][-1]:24.1e}  {bres['solve'][-1]:7.1e}")

How to read it. (a) The two normal-equation methods stay near the κ²ε line, the two methods that work on $\mathbf G$ stay near or below κε (numbers printed). At the largest κ shown, the normal equations have lost essentially all digits while QR and SVD still give many. For still larger κ, round-off can make $\mathbf G^\top\mathbf G$ numerically indefinite, and then its Cholesky factorisation fails outright (5e). (b) Even for the same normal-equation system, multiplying by an explicit inverse leaves a residual that grows with κ, while a solve keeps it at round-off level.

Common misreadings.

  • "Matrix inversion is how linear systems are solved." Libraries solve by factorisation (LU, Cholesky, QR); an explicit inverse is slower and less accurate. Write np.linalg.solve(A, b), scipy.linalg.cho_solve, or np.linalg.lstsq(G, d).
  • "The formulas in a paper say $(\mathbf G^\top\mathbf G)^{-1}$, so the code must form it." The formula says what is computed, not how. Small matrices (the 2 × 2 of section 4) are harmless to invert; regularisation (2.09) also improves the condition number, which is part of why it helps.

In a real slip inversion the condition number of $\mathbf G$ is often large because deep patches leave nearly identical, weak fingerprints; the next section shows the extreme case.

7. The SVD: rank, null space, and what the data cannot see¶

In plain words. The singular value decomposition splits any matrix, square or not, into independent channels: a slip pattern goes in, a data pattern comes out, multiplied by a gain (the singular value). Channels with large gain are well measured, channels with tiny gain are drowned in noise, and when there are more unknowns than data some slip patterns produce no data at all. Those invisible patterns form the null space.

Precisely. $\mathbf G = \mathbf U\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf V^\top$: columns of $\mathbf V$ (slip patterns) and of $\mathbf U$ (data patterns) are orthonormal, $\boldsymbol\Sigma$ holds the singular values $s_1\ge s_2\ge\dots\ge 0$, and $\mathbf G\mathbf v_i = s_i\mathbf u_i$. The singular values are the square roots of the eigenvalues of $\mathbf G^\top\mathbf G$. The rank is the number of nonzero $s_i$: the number of independent combinations of the unknowns that the data measure; it cannot exceed $\min(N_d, N_m)$. Every $\mathbf v_i$ with $s_i = 0$, and every combination of them, satisfies $\mathbf G\mathbf v = \mathbf 0$: that set is the null space. 2.07 uses the same decomposition for the least-squares solution and for truncated SVD.

Worked example. The same three stations, now with five patches from 0 to 25 km.

In [23]:
z5 = np.linspace(0.0, 25.0, 6)
G5f = 1000.0 * np.array([[patch_disp(x, z5[j], z5[j + 1]) for j in range(5)] for x in x_st])
U6, s6, Vt6 = np.linalg.svd(G5f)
rank6 = int(np.sum(s6 > s6[0] * 1e-12))
print("G (3 x 5), mm per m:\n", G5f)
print("singular values (mm per m):", s6, f"  rank = {rank6}; condition number of the nonzero part {s6[0] / s6[rank6 - 1]:.1f}")
null = Vt6[rank6:]                                                     # (5 - rank) x 5
print(f"null space: {null.shape[0]} independent slip patterns; |G v| for each:", np.abs(G5f @ null.T).max(0))
m_a = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 1.5, 0.5, 0.2])
m_b = m_a + 3.0 * null[0]
print("two very different slip models:", m_a, "and", np.round(m_b, 3))
print("their predictions (mm):", G5f @ m_a, "and", G5f @ m_b)

Common misreadings.


    

  • "With enough computing power we can solve for five patches from three stations." No amount of computing changes
the rank; the null space is a property of the experiment.
    • 

  • "A null-space pattern is noise." It is any slip, possibly large, that the stations cannot see.
    • 























8. The log-determinant: the Gaussian likelihood without overflow (optional)¶
In plain words. The Gaussian log-likelihood has two parts: the misfit, and a term that depends on the size of
the noise, $-\tfrac12\ln\det(2\pi\mathbf C_d)$. The second part matters whenever the noise level is estimated
(hierarchical models, 2.30). The determinant of a big covariance is an astronomically large or small number that a
computer cannot store; its logarithm is an ordinary number.


Precisely.
$\ln p(\mathbf d\mid\mathbf m) = -\tfrac12\mathbf r^\top\mathbf C_d^{-1}\mathbf r - \tfrac12\ln\det\mathbf C_d - \tfrac{N_d}{2}\ln 2\pi$.
With the Cholesky factor, $\ln\det\mathbf C_d = 2\sum_i\ln L_{ii}$ (5d); np.linalg.slogdet returns the same safely.
Computing np.log(np.linalg.det(C)) instead underflows to $-\infty$ or overflows to $+\infty$ once $N_d$ is large
(underflow: a number too small to store becomes 0; overflow: too large becomes infinity), and which one
happens depends on the units.


Worked example. Independent noise of σ = 2 mm at $N_d$ stations, written in metres and in millimetres.


















In [25]:






print("  N_d   units   det(C)        log(det(C))      slogdet         2 sum log L_ii    exact N ln sigma^2")
rows7 = []
for Nn in [10, 100, 300, 1000, 3000]:
    for unit, sg in [("m", 2e-3), ("mm", 2.0)]:
        C7 = sg ** 2 * np.eye(Nn)
        with np.errstate(divide="ignore", over="ignore"):
            dt = np.linalg.det(C7)
            ld_naive = np.log(dt)
        ld_slog = np.linalg.slogdet(C7)[1]
        ld_chol = 2 * np.sum(np.log(np.diag(np.linalg.cholesky(C7))))
        rows7.append((Nn, unit, ld_naive, ld_slog))
        print(f"{Nn:5d}   {unit:4s}  {dt:11.3e}   {ld_naive:13.4f}   {ld_slog:13.4f}   {ld_chol:13.4f}   {Nn * np.log(sg ** 2):13.4f}")

        txt = "finite" if ok else ("det = 0\nlog = −inf" if v < 0 else "det = inf\nlog = +inf")
        ax.text(col, row, ("✓ " if ok else "✗ ") + txt, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8,
                color=S.INK, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.35", fc=S.SURFACE, ec=S.GOOD if ok else S.BAD, lw=1))
ax.set_xlim(-0.6, len(Ns) - 0.4); ax.set_ylim(1.6, -0.6)
ax.set_xticks(range(len(Ns))); ax.set_xticklabels([str(n_) for n_ in Ns])
ax.set_yticks([0, 1]); ax.set_yticklabels(["σ = 0.002 m", "σ = 2 mm"])
ax.set_xlabel("number of data N_d")
for sp in ["left", "bottom"]:
    ax.spines[sp].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(length=0)
ax.set_title("(b) np.log(np.linalg.det(C)): the same noise, two units")
fig.tight_layout()
bk.savefig(fig, "2-06_logdet")
plt.show()

























saved figures/2-06_logdet.png




































How to read it. (a) The coloured lines (slogdet) grow in proportion to $N_d$ and agree with the exact value
$N_d\ln\sigma^2$ (printed); the open circles mark where the plain logarithm of the determinant is still finite.
(b) The plain route fails for the same noise level in both units: in metres the determinant underflows to 0, in
millimetres it overflows to infinity, at the station counts marked with a cross (printed table).


Common misreadings.


    

  • "The determinant term is a constant, so it never matters." It is constant only while $\mathbf C_d$ is fixed.
When a noise scale or a correlation length is estimated, it is the term that stops the noise from growing without
limit (2.29, 2.30).
    • 























Summary: from formula to code¶




on paper
in code
why






$\mathbf G\mathbf m$
G @ m
check shapes $(N_d\times N_m)(N_m)$ and units




$\mathbf A^{-1}\mathbf b$
np.linalg.solve(A, b)
an explicit inverse is slower and less accurate




$(\mathbf G^\top\mathbf G)^{-1}\mathbf G^\top\mathbf d$
np.linalg.lstsq(G, d)
the normal equations square κ




is $\mathbf C$ a valid covariance?
np.linalg.eigvalsh(C)
all ≥ 0; a clearly negative one means it is not




$\mathbf C = \mathbf L\mathbf L^\top$
L = np.linalg.cholesky(C) (add a tiny jitter only for round-off)
square root of a covariance




draw from $\mathcal N(\boldsymbol\mu,\mathbf C)$
mu + L @ z
correlated noise from independent noise




$\mathbf r^\top\mathbf C^{-1}\mathbf r$
sum(solve_triangular(L, r, lower=True)**2)
whitening; no inverse




$\ln\det\mathbf C$
np.linalg.slogdet(C)[1] or 2*sum(log(diag(L)))
no overflow




rank, null space
np.linalg.svd(G)
what the data can and cannot see






The image to keep. A matrix is a table of fingerprints. Its transpose sends residuals back to the parameters, a
covariance is read through its eigenvalues, its Cholesky factor makes, whitens and scores correlated noise, its SVD
lists what the data can see, and in code you solve rather than invert.
